The music is not good "for a toilet recording." The music is good. The saxophone lines have the melodic intelligence of someone who has spent years studying jazz harmony. The drum parts have the technical polish of someone who practices four hours a day. The interplay between the two musicians -- the way the sax responds to the drums, the way the drums anticipate the sax, the molecular-level communication that only happens between people who have played together extensively -- is the kind of thing that jazz critics rhapsodize about when it occurs in a club with good lighting and a well-tuned piano.

It occurs in a toilet.

* * *

Remove every external marker of seriousness from serious music. Take away the concert hall. Put the musicians in a van. Take away the van. Put them in a toilet. Take away their identities. Cover their faces with clown masks. Take away their dignity. Make them play in the space where people urinate. Take away every signal that tells the listener: this is art, these people are professionals who deserve your respect.

What's left?

The music. Just the music. The ghost notes and the blast beats and the saxophone screams and the precision and the conversation between two musicians who have known each other's playing for years, stripped of every external indicator that tells you how to feel about what you're hearing. You can't look at the setting and think: this must be serious, because I'm in a jazz club. You're watching a toilet. You can't look at the performers and think: these must be serious musicians, because they're wearing suits and have serious expressions. They're wearing clown masks. You have to listen. You have to actually hear the music, without the crutches of context and costume and prestige that normally tell your brain whether to take something seriously.

People do. Millions of people do.

The Russian literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin spent much of his career thinking about carnival -- not as entertainment but as epistemology. Carnival was the temporary suspension of all hierarchies: king becomes peasant, sacred becomes profane, the exalted is dragged down and the lowly is raised up. The inversion was not chaos. It was revelation. By flipping the social order, carnival exposed the order as arbitrary -- a set of agreements maintained by the people who benefited from them, not as natural law. Put the king in a jester's hat and the agreement wobbles.

Clown Core is carnivalesque in the most literal sense Bakhtin could have imagined. Clown masks -- the universal symbol of carnival. A portable toilet -- the lowest point in the spatial hierarchy of civilization. Virtuosic music -- the highest point in the hierarchy of human achievement. Smash them together. The concert hall becomes a toilet and the toilet becomes a concert hall, and the inversion reveals what Bakhtin always said it would reveal: that the hierarchy between the two is a social construction, maintained by institutions and critics and ticket prices and dress codes, not by anything intrinsic to the music itself. And unlike Bakhtin's carnival, which was temporary -- a release valve that ultimately reinforced the existing order -- Clown Core's carnival is permanent. The masks don't come off. The toilet doesn't get replaced by a proper studio. The inversion is not a holiday from the hierarchy. It is a refusal to acknowledge that the hierarchy exists.

Music critics and cultural analysts who have tried to explain Clown Core have noted that the duo "uses genre to satirise musicians and the fanaticism that comes with them." They take jazz, a style of music "synonymous with musical greats, various competitions, and high artistical merit," and deploy it in the lowest-status environment imaginable. If you need a concert hall to take jazz seriously, you don't actually take jazz seriously -- you take concert halls seriously, and jazz is just the excuse to go there.

Clown Core videos have accumulated views in the tens of millions. The "Toilet" video -- twelve minutes of two clowns playing jazz-metal in a portable toilet, published through Adult Swim's online "Smalls" program -- went viral in the way that only things that defy categorization go viral, shared by the algorithmic currents of Twitter and Reddit and TikTok, by people who saw the thumbnail and clicked because it promised something they'd never seen before, and then stayed because the music was undeniably, aggressively good.

* * *

The masks have a lineage. MF DOOM -- the late rapper Daniel Dumile, who performed in a metal mask inspired by Doctor Doom -- used anonymity as a narrative device. The mask wasn't a disguise; it was a character, a fictional persona that allowed Dumile to explore perspectives his own face would have anchored to autobiography. Daft Punk wore robot helmets that eliminated their humanity entirely, turning two French producers into a concept that could exist independently of the men behind it. GWAR bled on the audience. Buckethead's KFC bucket was, like much of Buckethead's existence, a question mark with a guitar.

But the deepest root of the family tree isn't in hip-hop or electronic music. It's in sixteenth-century Italy, and the connection isn't a metaphor. Commedia dell'arte: troupes of masked performers traveling between cities, improvising virtuosically around pre-set scenarios called *lazzi* -- comic bits, physical routines, musical interludes, all executed with the precision of athletes and the spontaneity of jazz musicians. The masks were not disguises. They were amplifiers. A commedia mask fixed the face into a single expression and by fixing the face, forced all expression into the body, the voice, the timing. The most controlled surface produced the most uncontrolled content. The actor couldn't raise an eyebrow. So the actor had to make you laugh with everything else.

Two clowns in a toilet, playing jazz-metal through latex masks that lock their faces into permanent grins, forcing all expression into the hands, the breath, the ghost notes, the molecular dynamics of stick on skin. The most controlled surface producing the most uncontrolled content. Commedia dell'arte with a distortion pedal. And the stoic driver? Commedia had a name for him too: the *vecchio* -- the straight man, the gravitational center that the clowns orbit. Pantalone sits at the front of the stage, dignified and immovable, while Arlecchino cartwheels behind him. The balaclava sits at the wheel, hands at ten and two, staring straight ahead, while the back of the Previa detonates. Same function. Same comedy. Five hundred years apart.

The masks allow two musicians with active, visible, public careers under their own names to do something they could not do with their faces showing: make the most ridiculous music imaginable, in the most ridiculous setting imaginable, with the most ridiculous visual presentation imaginable, and have it be taken seriously as art. Because it is art. The masks don't make it art -- the music makes it art. But the masks make the art legible, by providing a frame so deliberately absurd that the only thing left to respond to is the content. If Cole and Gendel stood in a toilet with their faces visible, the conversation would be about them. The masks redirect the conversation from the who to the what. The clowns can't be judged by their reputations, because the clowns don't have reputations. The clowns are just clowns. And the clowns play like gods.

* * *

In 2023, Clown Core performed at the Bimhuis in Amsterdam.

The Bimhuis is not a toilet. It is one of Europe's most respected jazz venues -- a purpose-built concert hall with impeccable acoustics, a curated program, and an audience that takes its music seriously. The kind of venue where you'd see a thoughtful quartet playing post-bop standards, or a European free-improvisation ensemble, or a visiting American soloist working through new material with a local rhythm section.

And here were two clowns. In a portable toilet. On the stage of one of Europe's most respected jazz venues.

The show opened with the toilet at center stage, sealed shut. From inside the plastic walls came sounds -- a clown horn, a snare hit, muffled and reverberant in the way that only a four-by-four-foot plastic enclosure can produce. The audience leaned forward in their seats. Then the front panels of the toilet fell open, revealing two figures in white tuxedos crammed into the portable toilet with a miniature drum kit -- tiny bass drum, hi-hats, snare, splash cymbal, two keyboards -- and a saxophone. The lighting was extreme: seizure warnings had been issued, strobe effects combined with CGI projections and live-streamed footage from inside the toilet. A multi-media production of the highest caliber, deployed in service of two men playing instruments in a toilet.

The Bimhuis audience, trained by decades of serious jazz, watched two clowns play jazz-metal-noise at volumes that tested the venue's acoustic design, and they responded the way Clown Core audiences always respond: with the variety of joy that occurs when your expectations are not just defied but annihilated, when the gap between what you thought was going to happen and what is happening is so wide that the only possible response is surrender.

There is a reading of Clown Core that is completely defensible once you think about it for ten seconds, and it goes like this.

Plato's allegory of the cave: prisoners chained in a cavern, watching shadows on a wall, believing the shadows to be reality. The philosopher escapes the cave, sees the sun, understands that the shadows were projections of real objects, and returns to tell the prisoners what he's seen. The prisoners don't believe him. They prefer the shadows. The allegory is about the difficulty of accepting that the world you know is not the world as it is.

Now invert it. Clown Core enters the cave voluntarily. They walk into the toilet -- the smallest, darkest, least prestigious space available -- and they close the door behind them. And there, in the cave, in the toilet, they play music of such blinding virtuosity that the question reverses itself. The question is no longer "how do you escape?" The question is: what if the cave is where the real things live?

Consider the possibility. The concert hall -- the Bimhuis, the Palacio de los Deportes, the purpose-built acoustic temple with its assigned seating and its ticket prices and its implicit dress code -- is Plato's wall. It is the surface on which we project our ideas about what serious music looks like. The tuxedos, the reverent silence, the program notes explaining what you're about to hear and how you should feel about it: these are the shadows. Agreeable, familiar, shaped by centuries of convention into forms we recognize and accept without question.

The toilet, stripped of every pretension, is the world outside the cave. The sunlight is harsh in there. The acoustics are terrible. There is no program note. There is no usher. There is only the music, and you, and your ability to hear it for what it is without anyone telling you what it is. The prisoners in the concert hall would not believe you if you told them. They prefer the shadows. The shadows have better lighting.

* * *

The Bimhuis shows -- March 2023, the final dates of Clown Core's first-ever world tour -- ended the way Clown Core shows always end: abruptly, without ceremony, with the toilet closing around the two clowns like a mouth swallowing its own tongue. The audience sat in one of Europe's finest jazz halls, surrounded by the acoustic architecture designed to make music sound as good as physics will allow, and watched two men close themselves inside a portable toilet and disappear. The applause was thunderous. The toilet was silent. Somewhere inside the plastic walls, two men in clown masks were sitting in the dark, probably sweating, definitely not talking about what it all means.

The nightmare in the toilet isn't a nightmare at all. It's the clearest possible expression of what Cole believes about music: that the only thing that matters is the sound, that every other element -- the venue, the outfit, the persona, the face -- is furniture, and furniture can be rearranged without changing what happens in the room. The toilet is a room. The van is a room. The Bimhuis is a room. The living room is a room. The constraint is the aesthetic — it always was, from the cardboard-box bass drum to the one-mic garage to the four-by-four-foot toilet, each limitation compressing the creativity into a denser and more volatile form. In every room, the same hands, the same ghost notes, the same precision, the same commitment. You can disguise your appearance, but you can't disguise your ghost notes, and ghost notes are as unique as fingerprints.

The mask comes off at the end of the show. Or it doesn't. Either way, the music was never behind the mask. The music was always in front of it, in the air between the instruments and the audience, in the space where vibrations become meaning. The clowns know this. The clowns have always known this.

And the toilet -- the tiny, plastic, undignified, acoustically terrible toilet -- turns out to have been a recording studio all along.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: The Brainfeeder Family
chapters.content:
The Blue Whale is a jazz club in Little Tokyo, Los Angeles. It sits on the second floor of a commercial building on East First Street, which means you climb a staircase to reach it, which means the music hits you in the stairwell before you see the room — bass frequencies traveling through concrete, the muffled pop of a snare, a piano bleeding through the ceiling like light through cracks. The room itself is small. Low ceiling. Close tables. The kind of jazz venue where you can see the pianist's hands from the back row, where the bass vibrates the floor under your feet, where the boundary between performer and audience is not a stage but a few feet of hardwood and a tacit agreement that everyone in the room is here because they care about the same thing.

On the night of November 20, 2012, the ensemble at the Blue Whale included Natasha Agrama on vocals, Dan Lutz on bass, Nick Mancini on vibes, and Louis Cole on drums. At the piano sat Austin Peralta.

They played Mingus's "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat" with Joni Mitchell's lyrics — a song about loss rendered in the language of two different geniuses, one who wrote the melody and one who heard words inside it. The performance was, by all accounts, exceptional. Peralta played the way he always played — with an intensity that seemed to exceed the physical capacity of his body to produce it, as though the music was larger than the instrument and the instrument was larger than the room and the room was straining at its walls to contain what was happening inside it.

"He was burning at maximum intensity," Cole said later. [SOURCE: FLOOD Magazine]

The sentence requires no gloss. It says what it says.

"It was a musical mutual understanding," Cole continued. "Everything he did made sense in the moment and felt right to me. It was a symbiotic vibe between the two of us." [SOURCE: FLOOD Magazine]

And then a smaller detail — one that breaks through the professional language and the critical frameworks and says something true about who these two people were to each other. During rehearsals the night before, they had discovered that "their sense of humor aligned." [SOURCE: FLOOD Magazine]

Two musicians, both in their twenties, both absurdly talented, both operating at the intersection of jazz and something else — finding common ground not in their vast musical vocabulary but in what made them laugh. The detail is the one that cracks the surface. These were two young guys who made each other laugh, and then one of them was gone.

Austin Peralta died on November 21, 2012. He was twenty-two years old.

The hours between the Blue Whale performance and the death are a gap no biography can fill. The jazz club on East First Street was still there the next morning, and the next week, and the next year — the same low ceiling, the same close tables, the same staircase where the bass bleeds through the concrete. But the room was different now, in the way that all rooms where someone played their last notes are different: still functional, still hosting music, still charging a cover and pouring drinks, but carrying an absence that is felt most acutely by the musicians who were in the room on the night it still mattered.

Cole was twenty-five. Peralta was twenty-two. They were both at the beginning of careers that seemed, from the vantage of November 2012, to have a long way to run. The symbiotic vibe. The musical mutual understanding. The humor that aligned. All of it, abruptly, became past tense — one of those ruptures that the living carry forward not as a lesson or a narrative but as weight, distributed unevenly across the years, settling into the hands and the gut and the spaces between the notes.

The drummer had to incorporate this loss into the body that sits behind the kit, into the hands that play the ghost notes, into the musical architecture of a career that owes its institutional foundation, in part, to a record that Peralta made before Cole even knew the label existed. Musicians who lose a collaborator don't process the loss the way other people do. Other people grieve with words, with rituals, with the passage of time. Musicians grieve with the same instrument they used to play together, and every time they sit down at the kit, the absence is there in the frequencies — the chord voicings that nobody else plays the same way, the harmonic conversation that used to go in a direction it can no longer go, the silence where the piano used to answer the drums.

The record Peralta left behind was called *Endless Planets*. And it changed everything.

* * *

*Endless Planets* was released in 2011 on Brainfeeder Records, and it was the label's first jazz release. The sentence needs context, because before *Endless Planets*, Brainfeeder was not a jazz label. Brainfeeder was Steven Ellison — Flying Lotus, Alice Coltrane's grandson — and it was beat music, experimental hip-hop, electronic psychedelia, the sound of Los Angeles filtered through laptop screens and low-end frequencies. Jazz was not on the menu.

Peralta put jazz on the menu. He was twenty years old.

"Maybe the most important record to me since I've been doing this," said Adam Stover, Brainfeeder's manager. "This is the catalyst for everything we've done." [SOURCE: FLOOD Magazine]

The catalyst. Stover is saying that a jazz record by a twenty-year-old pianist was the chemical agent that initiated every reaction that followed. Before *Endless Planets*, Brainfeeder released electronic music. After *Endless Planets*, Brainfeeder could release jazz. And by demonstrating that jazz could exist within Brainfeeder's ecosystem, could reach its audience, could live alongside the beat music without contradiction — Peralta opened a door. Through that door walked Kamasi Washington. Through that door walked Hiatus Kaiyote. Through that door, years later, walked Louis Cole.

The liner notes to *Endless Planets* include a statement that reads less like a dedication and more like a prophecy: "True art defies categorization and transcends boundaries... It can be the doorway into an infinitude of worlds."

The door Peralta opened stayed open. Everyone who walked through it walks through it still.

Listen to *Endless Planets*. The album opens with a track called "Epilogue," which is the kind of joke only a twenty-year-old pianist would make — the ending as the beginning, the whole story already told before it starts. The piano enters clean, almost classical, then bends into harmonies that sound like late Coltrane if late Coltrane had grown up with a laptop and a sense of humor about his own intensity. The rhythm section locks into grooves that are jazz in their harmonic language but electronic in their precision — the bass lines punching holes in the bottom end, the drums maintaining a kind of controlled restlessness that sounds, in retrospect, like a prophecy of what Brainfeeder's jazz catalog would become. The album is spiritual jazz made by someone young enough that the spirituality hasn't calcified into dogma. It breathes. It reaches. And underneath the reaching is a muscular rhythmic intelligence that explains why Flying Lotus heard it and said: this belongs on my label.

Brainfeeder, by this point, was five years old and already the most important experimental music label in Los Angeles — possibly in America. Ellison had started it in 2008 with releases from Samiyam, the Gaslamp Killer, and himself, the aesthetic defined less by genre than by a sensibility: music that was technically sophisticated and spiritually restless, that drew from jazz and hip-hop and electronic music without being reducible to any of them. The label's roster read like a map of the LA underground: Teebs, Tokimonsta, Thundercat, Ras G, Daedelus. What they shared was not a sound but an orientation — a willingness to make music that confused the algorithms, that didn't fit the playlists, that required the listener to decide for themselves what they were hearing.

This was the ecosystem that would eventually house Cole's music. Not Blue Note, with its clean studio recordings and its canonical lineage from Monk to Herbie. Not Stones Throw, with its sample-based archaeology and vinyl-collector nostalgia. Not Warp, with its British electronic formalism. Brainfeeder — a label whose name sounds like what it does: it feeds the brain, not the market. The fact that Cole's albums sit in the same catalog as Flying Lotus's *Cosmogramma* and Thundercat's *Drunk* and Kamasi Washington's *Harmony of Difference* tells you something that genre labels cannot: that this music comes from a community that values the weird, that trusts the artist, that would rather release something confusing and brilliant than something safe and profitable.

"They trust me and let me do whatever I want," Cole said of Brainfeeder. "They're just really supportive." [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018]

Trust, in the context of a record label, is usually a business term — conditional, contractual, with recourse. But Brainfeeder's trust sounds like the other kind. The kind that exists between people who have sat in each other's living rooms and heard each other play and know, without verification, that the work will be good because the person is good. The kind built not by contracts but by Dennis Hamm saying to Flying Lotus, in a conversation nobody recorded: he's the real thing.

In 2019, while working on *Flamagra* — the album that would become Brainfeeder's most visible release since Thundercat's *Drunk* — Flying Lotus called Louis Cole "super inspirational." [SOURCE: Flying Lotus, Twitter/X, Apr 2020]

The compliment is revealing not because it's unusual for musicians to praise each other, but because of the direction. Flying Lotus is Steven Ellison: Alice Coltrane's grandson, the founder of Brainfeeder Records, the architect of a label and a scene that has reshaped the boundaries of what gets called jazz in the twenty-first century. He is the person who built the house. And the person he calls "super inspirational" is a man who records in his living room with two microphones, who plays every instrument himself, who built his audience one YouTube upload at a time, and whose relationship to the Los Angeles music scene is best described as: present everywhere, central nowhere, indispensable to the whole thing in a way that only becomes visible when you draw the connections.

The connections are the story. To tell the story of Louis Cole's career without telling the story of the scene that incubated it would be like describing a tree without mentioning the soil. The tree is interesting — its shape, its reach, the way it bends toward light. But the tree didn't invent the soil. The soil was there first, and the soil was made of other things: decades of musical tradition, a handful of specific venues, a network of musicians who kept showing up in each other's living rooms, and a series of relationships that operated not through record labels or management companies but through the more ancient technology of one person saying to another: you have to hear this guy.

But how did Cole end up in front of the door Peralta opened? How did a man who recorded in his living room end up on the same label as Flying Lotus and Thundercat?

The answer is a chain of introductions so short it would fit on a napkin.

* * *

Dennis Hamm is where the chain begins.

Not because Hamm is the most famous musician in Los Angeles — he's not — but because Hamm is the most connected. He is an LA-based jazz pianist who has been playing professionally for more than thirty years, starting at age four. Attended Citrus College, then CSU Bakersfield. Has been Thundercat's keyboardist for over a decade. Has toured fifty-plus countries with Cole, Thundercat, Chris Cornell, Babyface. His name doesn't appear on magazine covers. His name appears in the credits, and the credits — if you read them the way an archaeologist reads sediment layers — tell you who built the world the famous people live in.

Cole met Hamm in 2009.

The year matters because 2009 is the year Cole had a degree from USC, a technique refined by Aaron Serfaty, ears rebuilt by Tony Williams, a pep talk from Jack Conte, and no particular career plan beyond the conviction that making music on YouTube was a legitimate life. He was playing gigs. He was meeting people. He was doing what musicians in Los Angeles have always done: showing up, playing well, hoping the right person was in the room.

Hamm was the right person. The mechanism of their meeting was characteristically ordinary — the specific circumstances lost to the fog of musicians' overlapping schedules, of sessions and gigs and rooms where you end up because someone texted you a time and an address. They met. They played. Something clicked — the rhythmic version of recognizing your own language in a foreign country.

And then Hamm introduced Cole to Thundercat.

And then Hamm introduced Cole to Flying Lotus.

And then — and this is the detail that illuminates the architecture of the entire scene — Flying Lotus asked Hamm if Cole would release on Brainfeeder. Not Cole. Hamm. FlyLo asked the intermediary, the connector, the pianist whose social function in the LA music ecosystem is equivalent to a nerve cell in a brain: carrying the signal from one node to another, making the circuit complete.

The chain: Cole → Hamm → Thundercat → FlyLo → Brainfeeder.

Four handshakes. That's all. Four handshakes between a man recording in his living room and the label that would release his music to the world. Not meetings in conference rooms with contracts and lawyers and the apparatus of the music industry as it is typically imagined. Four handshakes between musicians who had played together and trusted each other's ears and said, in the informal language of musicians everywhere: you have to hear this guy.

"They trust me and let me do whatever I want," Cole said of Brainfeeder. "They're just really supportive." [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018]

Trust, in the context of a record label, is usually a business term — conditional, contractual, with recourse. But Brainfeeder's trust sounds like the other kind. The kind that exists between people who have sat in each other's living rooms and heard each other play and know, without verification, that the work will be good because the person is good. The kind built not by contracts but by Dennis Hamm saying to Flying Lotus, in a conversation nobody recorded: he's the real thing.

The line from Dennis Hamm leads in one direction to Brainfeeder, to Flying Lotus, to the institutional framework that gave Cole's music international distribution and a Grammy nomination. But lines in a scene don't run in one direction. They branch. They intersect. They fold back on themselves and produce connections that look, from the outside, like coincidences but are really the inevitable product of a community small enough that everyone knows everyone and generous enough that everyone plays with everyone.

Follow the line from Hamm to Thundercat, and Thundercat leads you backward in time, to Austin Peralta calling him to the Del Monte Speakeasy to see "his friend from high school play." [SOURCE: Thundercat, Pigeons & Planes; corroborated KEXP, Apr 2020] His friend from high school. Not "one of the most technically accomplished multi-instrumentalists in Los Angeles." His friend. The language tells you how the scene works: not through résumés or EPKs but through the primal currency of friendship. Come see my friend play. That's the whole pitch. That's the mechanism that connected Thundercat to Cole, which connected Cole to FlyLo, which connected Cole to Brainfeeder, which connected Cole to the world.

* * *

To understand the soil that Peralta grew from, and that Cole grew from, and that the entire LA jazz renaissance grew from, you have to understand a weekly event that happened at a bar called the Airliner, in Lincoln Heights, for nearly twelve years.

Low End Theory was founded in October 2006 by Daddy Kev and Nocando, with original resident DJs including Nobody, Gaslamp Killer, and edIT. The name was a reference to A Tribe Called Quest's album — a nod to the hip-hop tradition that valued bass weight and lyrical substance in equal measure. Every Wednesday night, for nearly twelve years, more than six hundred parties in total. The event launched, incubated, or provided essential early exposure to a list of artists that reads like the table of contents of the last fifteen years of experimental music in Los Angeles: Flying Lotus, Thundercat, Odd Future, Baths, Glitch Mob, Daedalus.

What the list doesn't tell you is what the Airliner felt like on a Wednesday night.

The room was narrow and hot. The monitors ran loud enough that the bass compressed the air — not in the metaphorical way that music journalists use the word, but in the physical, pressure-change way that you felt in your sternum before your ears processed the frequencies. The kick drum from the monitors landed in your chest the way a fist lands in a pillow: firm, sudden, gone, then back. The darkness was the kind that makes strangers into an audience, the kind where you couldn't see the person next to you clearly but you could feel them nodding to the same beat, a room of bodies synchronized by a frequency that operated below the threshold of conscious hearing and above the threshold of physical sensation.

Flying Lotus described the early days as a "producer's lounge" [SOURCE: NPR, May 2010] — a place where beat-makers and musicians gathered not to perform for an audience but to exist in each other's presence, absorbing approaches the way you absorb a language by living in a country where it's spoken.

The final night was August 2018 — Tyler, the Creator and Tokimonsta performed. The event ended the way most important cultural institutions end: not with a collapse but with a recognition that the musicians it had incubated had outgrown the room, that the scene it had catalyzed was bigger than any single weekly event could contain. But here is the thing about weekly events that run for twelve years: they don't just launch careers. They train ears. Six hundred Wednesday nights is six hundred chances for a twenty-year-old producer to stand in a room where Flying Lotus is playing and absorb, through the sternum, what it means to make music that doesn't fit. The event dies. The ears don't. The ears go home and make music, and the music carries the Airliner's frequencies in its bones — the bass weight, the darkness, the pressure change, the physical fact of a room where nobody cared whether the algorithms could categorize what they were hearing.

Cole was not a Low End Theory regular. His music — the funk, the pop, the live drums and keyboards — didn't fit neatly into the beat-centric aesthetic that defined the event's early years. But the scene that Low End Theory created was the scene that produced Flying Lotus, which produced Brainfeeder, which produced the institutional home for Cole's music. The connection is environmental. Low End Theory was the weather system. Brainfeeder was the climate. Cole's music was one of the things that grew in it.

* * *

And there was another ecosystem, parallel and overlapping, that grew from a different root system but shared the same soil.

The West Coast Get Down is a musical collective centered around Kamasi Washington. The members — Washington, Stephen "Thundercat" Bruner, Cameron Graves, Miles Mosley, Ronald Bruner Jr., Brandon Coleman, Ryan Porter — first met in 1993, as teenagers, through the Multi-School Jazz Band program led by Reggie Andrews in Watts. They rehearsed at Locke High School and, on their own time, jammed in Kamasi Washington's father's garage — known within the community as "the Shack." Their proving ground was the World Stage in Leimert Park, a performance space co-founded in 1989 by the legendary drummer Billy Higgins and poet Kamau Daaood — the same Billy Higgins who played on Ornette Coleman's *The Shape of Jazz to Come*, who helped invent free jazz and then spent his later years creating a physical space in South Los Angeles where the next generation could learn what he'd learned.

"Jazz probably kept us out of trouble," Washington has said, "as it gave us a discipline and a reason to live life." [SOURCE: Dazed Digital, Jun 2020]

The KSL Sessions — a thirty-day recording marathon in December 2011 at Kingsize Soundlabs in Echo Park — distilled the collective's years of shared experience into a singular event. Ten AM to two AM, every day, for thirty days. Approximately 190 songs recorded. Six solo albums produced, including Washington's *The Epic*, which would become one of the most celebrated jazz releases of the 2010s. The sessions operated on a principle familiar to Cole: communal effort in a shared space, everybody playing on everybody else's tracks, the boundaries between individual projects dissolving in the heat of sustained creative contact.

The West Coast Get Down and Cole's circle are not the same group. The Venn diagram overlaps — Thundercat is a member of both, a bridge between the two ecosystems — but the aesthetic territories are distinct. Washington's collective draws from spiritual jazz, from the Coltrane-to-Pharoah lineage, from the South LA tradition that connects Leimert Park to Congo Square. Listen to *The Epic* — the album that emerged from those KSL Sessions — and you hear a full orchestral architecture, strings and choir and a tenor saxophone that sounds like it's trying to reach the ceiling and keep going. The music is communal by design: written for ensembles, performed by collectives, recorded in a room full of people feeding off each other's energy in real time. The aesthetic is maximalist in the social sense — more people, more instruments, more bodies in the room, the sound of a community channeling its shared history through a shared vocabulary.

Cole's world draws from funk, from electronic music, from Stevie Wonder and drum-and-bass and the particular sonic vocabulary of a person who learned to play in a bedroom with a cardboard box. Listen to *Time* — which would arrive in 2018, five years after those KSL Sessions — and you hear one person's vision executed by one person's hands, with collaborators invited in for specific moments, specific textures, then sent home while Cole sits in the living room layering and adjusting and mixing until the thing sounds exactly the way he hears it in his head. The aesthetic is maximalist in the sonic sense — more layers, more detail, more things happening in the frequency spectrum — but minimalist in the social sense. One person. Two microphones. The room where he sleeps.

Washington's music looks outward — toward the community, the tradition, the audience gathered to share an experience. Cole's music looks inward — toward the living room, the individual, the experience of being one person in a room with instruments and machines. "The only thing I can really nail is drums," Cole told Clash Magazine [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022], and the self-deprecation carries a structural truth: he builds his music outward from the drum chair, one instrument at a time, each layer added by the same pair of hands. The WCGD builds inward from the ensemble, the arrangement conceived for multiple bodies, the music requiring presence in a way Cole's never does. Both approaches produce extraordinary results. Neither is complete without the other's existence. The scene needs both — the communal and the solitary, the garage full of teenagers and the living room with one man and a metronome.

But the soil is the same. The living rooms are different, but the principle — that music happens in rooms, that the rooms are more important than the stages, that the real work of a scene is the work that happens between the performances — is shared. The Shack in Watts and Cole's living room in Central LA are separated by fifteen miles and half a century of musical tradition, but both operate on the same premise: that the family you choose is the family that makes the music possible.

And the person who proves it — the person whose body literally carries the connection between the two ecosystems — is Stephen Lee Bruner. Thundercat. He grew up with the WCGD. He played in Kamasi's orbit before Kamasi was Kamasi. He's on *Drunk*, which is a Brainfeeder record. He's on Kendrick's *To Pimp a Butterfly*, which is a post-jazz masterpiece that couldn't have existed without the LA scene's particular hybridization of hip-hop and improvised music. And he's on Cole's *Time*, playing bass with the fluid, overdriven tone that has become his signature — the instrument half guitar, half synthesizer, the notes bent and smeared until they occupy a tonal space that no other bassist in the world occupies.

When Cole needed a bass player for "Bus in These Streets" on *Drunk*, Thundercat didn't send him charts. He sent him the track. And Cole sat in his living room and played drums and keyboards over it, and Thundercat took what came back and said: yes. That's it. The process — remote, asynchronous, each musician adding to the other's work in their own room, on their own time — is the Cole method. The fact that it worked seamlessly with Thundercat tells you that the two ecosystems are not as distinct as they appear. The communal and the solitary. The Shack and the living room. The same language, spoken with different accents.

* * *

The family Cole chose is smaller than a collective and larger than a duo, and its boundaries shift depending on the project.

There is Genevieve Artadi — "my most trusted person to check anything I've worked on," Cole has said. "I just trust her ears so much." [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] The trust is specific, professional, and clearly something more — the trust of two people who have made music together since 2009, who built a band from Garageband demos and YouTube videos, who developed the kind of musical telepathy that only comes from playing together for so long that conscious communication becomes unnecessary. Artadi is not Cole's sidekick. She is the other half of a musical conversation that has been going on for fifteen years, and the conversation has produced some of the most original music of its era.

There is Sam Gendel — "I've known Sam Gendel for a really long time," Cole said. "We've always been in each other's lives musically." [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] The saxophonist who, behind the clown mask, screams through a toilet, and without it, makes ambient records that Pitchfork calls the sound of "LA's bubbling ambient jazz scene." Gendel spent a summer with Cole practicing "four or five hours every day" [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022] — two musicians locked in the kind of intensive shared woodshedding that produces a vocabulary no one else speaks. Think about what that means: four or five hours, every day, for an entire summer. Not rehearsing songs for a gig. Practicing. Playing together the way athletes drill together — running patterns, building reflexes, training the body to respond to the other person's body without the mediation of thought. By the end of that summer, Cole and Gendel could do things together that required no communication, no signal, no count-off. The music simply happened between them the way conversation happens between people who have known each other so long that the sentences anticipate themselves.

The distance between the Clown Core violence and the solo-record silence is a distance Gendel traverses with the ease of a person who accepts that the two modes are not contradictions but perspectives, the way a landscape looks different at noon and midnight but is the same landscape.

There is Sam Wilkes — "He gets really deep into the music and he learns it so deeply," Cole said of the bassist [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] — who appears on Knower recordings and in Cole's live band, whose own solo albums are meditations on what happens when you slow a bass guitar down until it becomes a texture rather than an instrument. To learn Cole's music "deeply" means not just the notes but the logic underneath them — the architectural intention, the reason this ghost note falls here and not there, the reason this chord voicing sits this way and not another. The learning requires the kind of immersion that only happens between people who trust each other enough to be in each other's living rooms.

There is Dennis Hamm, who was there at the beginning.

And there is Jacob Mann, and Nate Wood, and Chris Fishman, and Ben Wendel, and the rotating cast of musicians who appear on Cole's albums and in his shows and in his living room — each one a node in a network that has no center and no edge, that extends in every direction from every living room and garage in Los Angeles, connecting musicians who might never share a stage but who share a city and a set of values and a willingness to show up when someone says: I need a bassist for this thing, can you come over Tuesday?

* * *

The scene is not a scene. A scene implies a location, a style, a moment in time with a beginning and an end. What exists in Los Angeles is something more like a mycelial network — the underground root system of a forest, where the trees look like individual organisms but are connected, beneath the surface, by threads of fungus that share nutrients and information in every direction. Each tree is independent. Each tree has its own shape, its own height, its own relationship to sunlight. But the trees are not alone. They are networked. They share resources. The health of one affects the health of all.

Cole is one tree in this forest. He draws from the shared root system — the traditions, the relationships, the accumulated knowledge of a city that has been producing jazz musicians for a century — and he contributes to it, by playing on other people's records, by showing up at other people's gigs, by opening his living room to sessions that will never be released but that maintain the connections, that keep the fungal threads alive.

Cole knows this. He knows his place in the network, and the knowledge carries neither false modesty nor inflated self-regard — just the clear-eyed assessment of a person who has been paying attention to his own ecosystem for fifteen years.

"Jazz is so cool because it's full freedom in the moment," he told Passion of the Weiss. [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] The statement is descriptive, not nostalgic. He is not eulogizing jazz or arguing for its relevance in the way that institutional jazz advocates do, with their NEA grants and their Lincoln Center galas. He is describing what it feels like from the inside: the freedom. The in-the-moment quality. The fact that when you play jazz with people you trust, the music goes places that no amount of solitary composition could reach. This is what the scene gives him that the living room cannot. The living room gives him control. The scene gives him surprise — the harmonic direction he didn't expect, the rhythmic conversation he couldn't have scripted, the experience of being inside a musical event that exceeds the sum of its participants.

"It's kind of a really weird skillset that I have," he told Clash Magazine. [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022] The sentence is Cole in concentrate: the self-deprecation that is actually a precise description, the humor that is actually an insight. His skillset IS weird — a jazz drummer who makes pop-funk records alone in his living room, who plays every instrument on his albums, who conducts a fifty-piece orchestra, who screams inside a portable toilet in a clown mask, who practices four hours a day and writes music seven hours a day and uploads videos to YouTube in which nothing about his face suggests that what he's doing is extraordinary. The weirdness is the point. The scene that produced him is full of weird skillsets, full of musicians who don't fit the categories their conservatory training prepared them for, who make music that the algorithms cannot classify, who found each other in living rooms and garages because the music industry had no category for what they do.

He is not the tallest tree. He is not the oldest. He is not the one with the deepest roots. But he is one of the most distinctive — his shape is his own, his music is his own, his approach to the instrument and the recording studio and the internet is so specifically, unmistakably his that you could blindfold a person and play five seconds of any Louis Cole recording and they would know. The distinctiveness is what made the YouTube videos work. The distinctiveness is what caught Anthony Kiedis's ear. The distinctiveness is what made Flying Lotus ask Dennis Hamm — not Cole, Hamm — whether Cole would be interested in releasing on Brainfeeder.

But the distinctiveness grew from the network. It grew from the soil. It grew from the years of showing up and playing and absorbing the language of the musicians around him, then going home to his living room and translating that language into something that sounded like nobody else. The tree is distinctive because the root system is rich, and the root system is rich because a hundred musicians across a hundred living rooms have been feeding it with their work, their presence, their willingness to say: you have to hear this guy.

"How did I just find all these people that sound like this? It's crazy," Cole told Clash Magazine. [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022] The sentence contains genuine wonder — the wonder of a person who understands that his own creative development is inseparable from the environment that produced it, that the family he found was itself a kind of instrument, a collective mechanism for making each individual member better than they would have been alone. He didn't find them. They found each other. The scene found itself, the way scenes always find themselves: one musician at a time, one living room at a time, one phone call that says come over Tuesday.

* * *

Thundercat, speaking to NPR about Cole, said three things that tell you everything about how the scene sees him.

"Louis Cole is, I think, one of Los Angeles's greatest musicians." [SOURCE: NPR, Aug 2024]

The superlative is not casual. Thundercat's professional circle includes Kamasi Washington, Herbie Hancock, Kendrick Lamar, and Flying Lotus. The verdict is delivered by a musician whose standards are set at the highest altitude the contemporary scene offers: Cole belongs at the top.

"He is 100% in control of what he's doing." [SOURCE: NPR, Aug 2024]

The emphasis is on the percentage. Not "very in control." A hundred percent. Thundercat is describing, in the language of a musician who understands what control costs, the product of the four hours of daily practice, the metronome under the pillow, the years of refining a relationship to time so precise that the distinction between the human and the machine becomes academic. Every ghost note is where he wants it. Every dynamic is calibrated. Every silence is chosen.

"What you're doing is definitely changing the world. Just keep going." [SOURCE: NPR, Aug 2024]

Not "your music is great." Not "I enjoy your work." What you're doing is *changing the world.* The scope is enormous — world-changing, said by a musician who has made world-changing music himself. And the imperative that follows — "just keep going" — is the instruction every artist needs to hear and almost never does, at least not from someone whose opinion carries this weight. Keep going. The work matters. The world is different because of it.

Three quotes. Three sentences. Each one escalating in scope: from the city (greatest musician in Los Angeles) to the skill (100 percent control) to the planet (changing the world). The trajectory of the praise mirrors the trajectory of the career — local, then precise, then global. And all three delivered not in a private conversation between musicians but on NPR, to a national audience, in a voice that carries the authority of a man who has played with everyone and is telling you, publicly and without hedging, that this is the one.

The praise is the network's praise for one of its nodes. The forest saying: this tree matters. Not because this tree is the forest. Because this tree, by being distinctly and stubbornly itself — by growing in its own shape, at its own pace, in its own living room — has contributed something to the canopy that wasn't there before.

* * *

Draw the map.

Take a map of Los Angeles — the real map, the one that includes Silver Lake and Echo Park and Lincoln Heights and Leimert Park and Watts and Hollywood and the unnamed neighborhoods between them. Draw a dot on every living room, every garage, every rehearsal space where a musician in this scene has made something or played something or shown up on a Tuesday to lay down a bass part on someone else's demo.

Draw lines between the dots. Not highways. Relationships. The I-met-her-through-him connections, the she-sat-in-on-that-session introductions, the chains of trust that carry one musician into another musician's orbit. Draw a line from Cole's living room to Hamm's piano. From Hamm's piano to Thundercat's bass. From Thundercat's bass to the Del Monte Speakeasy, where Peralta called him to come see "his friend from high school play." [SOURCE: Thundercat, Pigeons & Planes; corroborated KEXP, Apr 2020] From the Speakeasy to the Blue Whale in Little Tokyo, where the last performance happened. From the Blue Whale to the Airliner in Lincoln Heights, where Low End Theory ran for twelve years and launched the careers that created the label that gave Cole's music a home.

From the Airliner to Flying Lotus's apartment, where the label started — "It all started really just from my apartment," FlyLo said, "working with Samiyam and having him be my next-door neighbour." [SOURCE: Crack Magazine, Jul 2023] From the apartment to Kingsize Soundlabs in Echo Park, where the West Coast Get Down recorded 190 songs in thirty days. From Kingsize to the Shack in Watts, where teenagers connected through the Multi-School Jazz Band began playing together in 1993 and never stopped.

Every line passes through at least one of the same fifteen musicians. The network is smaller than it looks and exactly as interconnected as it needs to be — dense enough that the signal travels quickly, sparse enough that each node maintains its own identity, its own aesthetic, its own living room.

And Cole's living room is one of those nodes. Not the center. There is no center — that's the point. A mycelial network has no center. A forest has no center. An LA jazz scene that grew from a hundred living rooms and a weekly event at a bar and a dead pianist's first record and a phone call that said "come see my friend from high school play" — this scene has no center. It has nodes. It has connections. It has lines between dots that, if you drew them all, would look less like a circuit diagram and more like a root system, tangled and organic and alive.

Cole's thread runs through the middle of it. Through the living room where the music is made, through the garage where the drums are practiced, through the YouTube channel where the videos are uploaded, through the Brainfeeder catalog where the albums are released, and back — always back — to the living room. The family he chose made the music possible. The music he made gave the family another reason to exist.

One of those lines on the map runs from the Blue Whale in Little Tokyo, on the night of November 20, 2012, through every handshake and introduction and living-room session that followed, all the way to a Brainfeeder catalog number and a Grammy nomination and a fifty-piece orchestra playing compositions written in a garage. The line begins with two musicians playing together in a small room with a low ceiling — a pianist burning at maximum intensity and a drummer whose ghost notes fell between the chords like punctuation marks in a language only they spoke. They played Mingus. They made each other laugh. One of them died the next day. The other kept playing.

The Blue Whale is still there, on the second floor of a building on East First Street. The bass still bleeds through the stairwell. The room is still small enough that you can see the pianist's hands from the back row. Other musicians play there now — musicians who walked through the door that Peralta opened, who carry his influence the way you carry the influence of anyone who showed you what was possible before they were gone. The ghost in the scene is not a metaphor. The ghost is a twenty-two-year-old pianist who recorded the first jazz album on a label that would eventually release *Time* and *Quality Over Opinion* and *nothing*, and whose liner notes said "True art defies categorization and transcends boundaries," and who died the day after playing with a drummer who would spend the next decade proving those words right.

The door is still open. The music that travels through it carries Peralta's fingerprints alongside everyone else's. And somewhere at one of the nodes — in a living room in Central Los Angeles, behind an eighteen-inch bass drum, facing two microphones and a window that lets in the particular light that Southern California produces without apparent effort — a man who is 100 percent in control of what he's doing is playing the music that the family made possible.

The family is listening. The family is always listening.

They're in the next room.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Time
chapters.content:
Put on headphones. Good ones — the kind that sit around the ear, not in it, the kind that seal you off from the room you're sitting in, so that the only room you hear is the one inside the recording. Press play on *Time*, Louis Cole's first album on Brainfeeder, released August 10, 2018. The first track is called "Weird Part of the Night."

What hits you first is the drums. Not the volume — the drums aren't loud. What hits you is their closeness. The snare sounds like it's being played inside your skull, a dry crack without reverb, without the spacious wash that most producers apply to make a drum recording sound like it happened in a real room. This drum recording doesn't sound like it happened in a real room. It sounds like it happened in YOUR room — as though the drummer is sitting four feet away, on the other side of your desk, and the microphone is exactly where your head is.

Then the bass enters. Not an electric bass through an amplifier — a synth bass, thick and woolly, sitting underneath the drums like a foundation slightly too large for the house above it. The bass and the kick drum occupy the same frequency territory, and in most productions this would be a problem — a muddiness, a competition for space. Here it's a decision. The bottom end is dense because Cole wanted it dense. The groove is heavy because the weight is the point.

Then the keyboards, high and tight, stabbing chords that sit on top of the groove like sparks off a fire. Then the voice — Cole's voice, flat, close, multi-tracked into harmonies that sound like a choir of one person, which is what they are. The voice doesn't emote. The voice reports. The voice conveys the melody the way a GPS conveys directions: accurately, without investment in whether you follow them.

Fourteen tracks. Fifty-three minutes. This is what a living room in Los Angeles sounds like when it's been used as a recording studio for nearly a decade — not a converted living room, not a treated acoustic space, but a room where someone lives and also makes music, and the music carries the room's fingerprint the way a photograph carries the light's. The ceiling is in the reverb. The walls are in the ambience. The window is in the upper frequencies, where the glass subtly colors the reflections. Every Louis Cole record is, among other things, a portrait of a room.

* * *

The first track is called "Weird Part of the Night."

The title tells you something about Cole's relationship to his debut on a respected label. Most artists, given their first release on Brainfeeder — the label that has released Flying Lotus, Thundercat, Kamasi Washington — would open with a statement of intent. The biggest track. The most impressive production. The sonic equivalent of walking into a room and announcing: I belong here. Cole opens with a track that suggests arrival at a party after the interesting things have already happened, when the conversation has gotten strange and the responsible people have gone home.

Cole was thirty-one. He had been recording in his living room for eight years, building an audience one upload at a time, playing every instrument himself, releasing into the void. And now, for the first time, his music carried someone else's logo — not a major label's, but one that meant something to the musicians and critics who cared about the territory between jazz and everything else.

Brainfeeder gave Cole distribution. It gave him reach. What it didn't give him was direction. "They trust me and let me do whatever I want," he said. [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] What he wanted was to make a Louis Cole album — the same kind of album he'd always made, in the same room, with the same sensibility. The difference was that this time, a few friends came over.

* * *

Brad Mehldau plays piano on "Real Life."

The sentence needs a moment to settle, because Brad Mehldau — who has spent three decades redefining the jazz piano trio, whose *Art of the Trio* series is among the most celebrated recording achievements in modern jazz — played piano on a Louis Cole track. In Cole's living room. On a record that also contains tracks called "After the Load Is Blown" and "Freaky Times."

Cole's account of the session was characteristically laconic. "He played a really sick piano solo on 'Real Life,'" he told Gigwise. [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018] Sick. That's the word Cole chose to describe Brad Mehldau's contribution to his debut on a respected label. The way you might describe a skateboarding trick or a particularly good sandwich.

What Mehldau actually plays is something you can listen to twenty times and still not fully process. The solo enters at the bridge, where the track's groove locks into a post-bop harmonic framework and Mehldau pushes against it with increasing force, the notes accelerating through the changes with the kind of abandon that only musicians who are very, very good allow themselves. Mehldau's reputation is built on coolness — the kind of controlled intensity that suggests a furnace behind a glass wall. On "Real Life," the glass breaks. The solo careens with a freedom that comes from confidence, and confidence comes from ten thousand hours, and Mehldau has those hours the way Cole has those hours, and the two sets of hours meet in a living room in Los Angeles. The piano's overtones bounced off walls close enough to touch — the sustain pedal humming through the floor, the sound folding back on itself in a space too small for the talent it contained.

Thundercat appears on "Tunnels in the Air." Dennis Hamm appears on "Trying Not to Die." Genevieve Artadi appears on "When You're Ugly." The guest list is a map of the scene described in the previous chapter — the overlapping circles, the living-room-to-living-room connections. Every guest is someone Cole knows, someone he has played with, someone he has sat in a room with and trusted. The album is not a showcase of collaborators. It is a recording of friendships.

* * *

The string arrangements on *Time* are one of the album's least discussed and most revealing elements.

Cole brought in a twenty-three-person string ensemble from Rochester, New York. [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018] Twenty-three classical musicians flew across the country to play on a record being made in a garage. The sessions were conducted to a click track — the string players couldn't hear the rest of the music. They played their parts blind, trusting the notation and the metronome, without knowing what the finished context would sound like. Cole conducted them — a man with no formal training in orchestral direction, conducting twenty-three conservatory-trained musicians playing parts he had written for instruments he barely played.

In a separate session, a trio of string players recorded in the living room itself. Close. Intimate. The same room, the same microphones, the same proximity that defines every Cole recording.

And on the final track, "Night," Cole picked up a violin and played it himself. [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018] Not well, by conservatory standards. But the point of "Night" is not virtuosity. The point is the texture of a person playing an instrument they haven't mastered — the slight uncertainty in the bowing, the human imprecision that a professional violinist would eliminate and that Cole kept, because the wobble IS the feeling, and the feeling is the album's last word. The track closes *Time* the way a hand closes around something fragile: gently, imperfectly, with visible effort.

The string sessions reveal something about Cole's production philosophy that his own descriptions tend to obscure. "I wanted it crusty on purpose because it grooves way harder," he told Gigwise. [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018] Crusty. The word is doing serious work. A crusty recording is one where the distortion, the imprecision, the roughness have been left in — not as accidents but as choices, the sonic equivalent of an unfinished edge on a piece of furniture that tells you a human hand was involved. The crustiness is not a limitation. The crustiness is the warmth. The crustiness is what makes the album sound like it was made by a person in a room, rather than by software in a server.

* * *

Making a record, for Cole, is a war of attrition against his own judgment.

"Doing an album is such a mental game," he told Gigwise. "You have to somehow still love your music through the whole process — and that's fucking hard, man." [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018]

The sentence is the most candid thing Cole has said about the cost of his practice. Not the financial cost, not the time cost, but the psychological cost — the experience of spending months with your own material, hearing it hundreds of times, losing the ability to hear what's good about it because familiarity has flattened everything into a featureless plain of sound you can no longer evaluate with fresh ears.

"I went through so many times where I just thought the music sucked and of course later I realised I loved it still." [SOURCE: Gigwise, Nov 2018]

The oscillation — love it, hate it, love it again — is not unique to Cole. It's the experience of every artist who spends extended time with their own work. But Cole's oscillation has a particular intensity because the work is made in isolation. There is no band to reassure you. There is no producer to say it sounds good. There is no engineer shaking their head in admiration while adjusting the fader. There is you, in a room, listening to the same eight bars for the fortieth time, trying to determine whether the thing you've made is brilliant or garbage, and the room offers no opinion, and the microphone offers no opinion, and the walls are exactly as close as they were an hour ago when you were certain it was brilliant and now you're certain it's garbage and the only thing that hasn't changed is the music.

"The main battle for me is always getting myself to be cool with it," he told Passion of the Weiss. [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018]

Cool with it. Not ecstatic. Not proud. Cool with it — the baseline acceptance that allows a person to stop working on something and release it. Cole's albums are not the product of inspiration. They are the product of a person fighting his own quality standards until the standards are met, or until the proximity to the standards is close enough that releasing the work is preferable to another month of fighting. Every album is a negotiation between the musician and the perfectionist, and the musician wins only when the perfectionist is too exhausted to object.

* * *

The album is called *Time*.

Not a metaphor. A subject. The same word that describes what Cole practices four hours a day, the thing he told Modern Drummer he focuses on exclusively, the fundamental relationship between a drummer's internal pulse and the music's external pulse. *Time* is what makes a groove breathe or suffocate, what separates the mechanical from the musical, what takes years to develop and seconds to lose.

"Time is the coolest thing that you can have," Cole told the Line of Best Fit. "There's nothing greater. Except maybe inspiration." [SOURCE: Line of Best Fit, Apr 2019]

The qualifier is telling. Time — the drummer's sense of time, the metronomic internal clock that governs every note — is the thing Cole practices. Inspiration is the thing he can't practice. Time is the craft. Inspiration is the mystery. Time is the hours. Inspiration is what sometimes happens during the hours, uninvited, unexplained, the thing that turns a practice session into a song. The album is named after the thing you can control. The best parts of the album come from the thing you can't.

Fourteen tracks. Every note played or programmed by Cole, with the exception of the guest features. Mixed in the living room, on headphones, in the room whose acoustic fingerprint is embedded in every frequency. The recursion is the point. An album called *Time* made by a man who practices time, made in a room where time is the primary raw material. The title is the thesis. The thesis is the practice. The practice is the album. The album is called *Time*.

* * *

The critics heard it. Mostly.

Pitchfork gave *Time* a 7.6 out of 10 and described it as "an unusual mixture of hard funk and soft pop, like Zapp and Burt Bacharach stuck in an elevator together." The image is exactly right and exactly wrong. Right, because the sonic territory is accurately mapped — *Time* oscillates between mechanical funk and tender pop, between beats that could power a dance floor and melodies that could score a wedding. Wrong, because the image suggests accident — Zapp and Bacharach didn't choose to be in this elevator — when the combination is deliberate, the product of a person who listened to James Brown and the Beach Boys with equal intensity and decided the two traditions could coexist if you just let them.

The Healthy Music Obsession review cut closer to the truth, calling the album "an expression of genuine emotion in an aesthetic that has garnered a reputation for a lack of emotionality" and "an ecstatic, heart-thumping listening experience." The sentence identifies the central paradox — the dry production, the flat affect, the controlled presentation, all of it sheltering musical content that is, if you listen past the packaging, deeply earnest. "Last Time You Went Away" is a love song. "More Love Less Hate" is exactly what the title says. "Trying Not to Die" — Dennis Hamm's piano alongside Cole's voice — is about the experience of being alive, the most sincere subject possible, delivered in a production style so dry that the sincerity arrives as surprise. You don't expect the man in the skeleton suit to mean it. He means it.

What neither review mentioned — what reviews rarely mention, because the vocabulary of music criticism is built for the ears, not the body — is what the album does below the neck. Put on "Trying Not to Die" at volume. Dennis Hamm's piano enters over a groove so deep and so patient that it doesn't so much reach your head as settle into your chest, a rhythm that your sternum recognizes before your ears have finished processing the chord voicings. Your head nods. Not because you decided to nod — the nod is involuntary, a muscular response to a rhythmic stimulus, the way your knee jerks when the doctor taps it. The ghost notes between the main snare hits are what's doing it. They're too quiet to hear consciously, but your body hears them, the way your body hears the difference between a metronome and a human pulse. The metronome is regular. The human pulse is alive. Cole's ghost notes are what make the regularity feel alive, and your body responds to aliveness the way it responds to all rhythmic stimuli — by moving, without permission, without deliberation, without any instruction from the critical apparatus that has opinions about whether the album deserves a 7.6 or a 9 or a perfect ten.

Jazzwise gave it three stars out of five and called it "playful, by turns annoying and thrilling" with a "chameleon-esque sound palette." AllMusic called it Cole's "most refined batch of animated pop yet." The Line of Best Fit gave it a 6 out of 10 and compared "After the Load Is Blown" to Prince — apt but insufficient. Prince used sexual provocation as a delivery system for musical genius. Cole uses sexual banality — the title is exactly what you think it is — as a delivery system for production genius. The track is lush, layered, beautiful in the way Prince's late-period ballads were beautiful: the kind that reveals itself only on repeated listening, because the first listen is occupied by the recognition that a track with this title is, in fact, one of the most gorgeous things you've heard all year.

Metacritic aggregated the reviews at 81 out of 100 — "universal acclaim." The number represents a critical consensus that hadn't quite figured out what to do with Cole. The reviews praised the musicianship, noted the humor, admired the production, and struggled to place the result in a category that already existed. The filing cabinet had drawers labeled "jazz" and "funk" and "electronic" and "pop," and *Time* didn't fit in any of them, and the reviewers — who are paid, essentially, to sort music into drawers — did their best.

What the reviews couldn't capture — what no review can capture — is what the album did to the living room. Before *Time*, Cole recorded for an audience that found him on YouTube. After *Time*, he recorded for an audience that Brainfeeder introduced him to — the Thundercat fans, the FlyLo listeners, the people who read Pitchfork and trusted its numerical verdicts enough to give a 7.6 thirty minutes of their headphone time. The audience grew. The room didn't. The microphone didn't. The eighteen-inch kick drum didn't. The gap between the size of the audience and the size of the room where the music was made grew wider with every review, every playlist addition, every person who put on "Weird Part of the Night" and thought: why does this sound like it's happening in my house?

Because it was recorded in a house. That's the answer. That was always the answer.

* * *

Four years later: *Quality Over Opinion*.

The title is a thesis statement aimed outward. *Time* was personal — here is what I practice, here is who I am, here is what my living room sounds like. *Quality Over Opinion* is polemical — here is what I believe about making art, and what I believe is that the work itself matters more than what anyone says about it. Including you. Including me. Including the Grammy voters who will nominate this album and then give the award to someone else.

"This album is a representation of me trying to make the best, most powerful and listenable music I can," Cole told BroadwayWorld. [SOURCE: BroadwayWorld, Nov 2023] The sentence is his plainest artistic statement — no irony, no deflection. Just the ambition, stated. Best. Most powerful. Most listenable. Three superlatives from a man who usually communicates in a register closer to a shrug.

When asked about his influences, Cole listed: Mahler. Ligeti. Miles Davis. Meshuggah. Morten Lauridsen. Super Mario Kart.

The list is a biography in six names. Mahler: the orchestral romantic who built symphonies as emotional architectures. Ligeti: the avant-gardist whose micro-polyphonic choral works were used in *2001: A Space Odyssey* because they sounded like the universe thinking. Miles Davis: the man who reinvented jazz every decade. Meshuggah: the Swedish metal band whose polyrhythmic grooves are among the most complex in modern music. Morten Lauridsen: the choral composer whose *O Magnum Mysterium* is among the most performed sacred works of the twenty-first century. And Super Mario Kart: the game.

The influences don't contradict. They accumulate. Each one represents a commitment to excellence pushed to its limit, and the fact that Cole can hold all six in his head simultaneously — listing a Swedish metal band and a Super Nintendo game alongside Mahler without apology or irony — tells you everything about how his creative mind organizes itself. There are no hierarchies. There is only quality. And quality, in Cole's vocabulary, is something you hear in Ligeti's *Atmosphères* and also in the Rainbow Road theme, and if you think the second doesn't belong in the same sentence as the first, that's an opinion. And quality is over opinion.

The title track is a manifesto delivered at speed — what All About Jazz called a "ratatat stream-of-thought over lush electronic symphony," Cole's voice rapid-firing his creative philosophy over production so dense it takes multiple listens to parse the layers. [SOURCE: All About Jazz, Feb 2024] All About Jazz called Cole "a chameleonic genius — merging beats, samples and catchy tunes across styles ranging from 'metal-funk-fusion' to 'pastoral falsettos.'" Song Bar called the album "brilliantly clever, agile and innovative" and noted how it alternated between "fast, perky beats and falsetto with slower, more tender love songs." [SOURCE: Song Bar, Oct 2022] The Guardian deemed it Cole's "most accomplished and well-rounded work to date." [SOURCE: The Guardian]

The dark-to-light oscillation — the rapid mood shifts that move from euphoric funk to a ballad so tender it sounds like it's apologizing for the volume of the previous track — is not a structural gimmick. It's a recording of what it feels like inside Cole's nervous system. "In real life, I experience that, those ups and downs," he told Passion of the Weiss. "I go from dark to light a lot in a short period of time." [SOURCE: Passion of the Weiss, Oct 2018] The album doesn't manage these shifts or smooth their edges. It presents them with the directness of a person saying: this is what it's like in here.

"The root of jazz is pure freedom," Cole said. "No limits... just what you're thinking right at that moment." [SOURCE: BroadwayWorld, Nov 2023]

Freedom within structure. Pure expression channeled through meticulous production. Cole needs absolute control to access absolute freedom. The walls of the living room are the constraint that makes the music possible. The obsessive mixing is the framework that allows the spontaneity to register. You build the cage so the thing inside it can fly.

"It's kind of a really weird skillset that I have," he told Clash Magazine. [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022] The self-assessment is delivered the way you might describe your blood type. A really weird skillset. The man who listed Ligeti and Super Mario Kart as equal influences calling his own abilities weird — not "unique," not "groundbreaking," not any of the words musicians reach for when discussing their talent. Weird. The way a platypus is weird: improbable, not designed by committee, functional in a way that doesn't match any existing blueprint.

Put on "Bitches." The track opens with a bass tone so dark and heavy it suggests a boiler room rather than a living room — the kind of frequency that doesn't register so much in the ears as in the lower spine, a seismic rumble over which Cole builds a groove that evokes Miles Davis circa 1970, the electric, menacing Miles of *On the Corner* and *Agharta*, the Miles who abandoned melody in favor of texture and made texture feel like a threat. The kick drum pattern is irregular, off-grid, landing in places that your body anticipates before your brain can map. Over this — without transition, without warning — Cole's falsetto enters, high and thin and sweet, floating above the darkness like a paper lantern over a factory floor. The contrast is violent. The darkness and the sweetness occupy the same track the way they occupy the same person, and the track makes no effort to reconcile them because reconciliation would be dishonest. Two tracks later, something that could have been written for a Japanese video game — bright, melodic, the harmonic language of a world where everything resets when you die and the worst thing that happens is a jaunty failure animation. The whiplash is the album.

"It does happen. It's not that often. It's most of the time. I think I'm just happiest when I'm working on something musical," he told Clash. [SOURCE: Clash Magazine, Oct 2022] The sentence circles back on itself the way his albums do — an assertion, a qualification, a reversal, and then the truth: most of the time. He is happiest most of the time, because most of the time he's working on something musical, and working on something musical is the only thing he does. The album documents a person who has eliminated from his life everything that isn't this, and the result is music so dense and varied that it sounds like the output of a collective, not one man in a room with a microphone and an opinion about quality.

* * *

The Grammy machine noticed. Twice.

In 2023, at the 65th Grammy Awards, "Let It Happen" — a single track from *Quality Over Opinion* — was nominated for Best Arrangement, Instruments and Vocals. The nomination placed Cole's living-room production in the same category as arrangements by Vince Mendoza, whose work with major orchestras represented the most polished institutional end of the music industry. Mendoza won, for his arrangement of "Songbird" in tribute to Christine McVie. Cole's nomination was both an honor and a parenthesis: we see you, we put you in the room, the room has assigned seating, your seat is over there.

One year later, at the 66th Grammy Awards, *Quality Over Opinion* was nominated for Best Alternative Jazz Album — a brand-new category in its inaugural year, a taxonomy invented to accommodate music that was obviously jazz-adjacent but didn't fit the existing categories, which had been designed for acoustic trios and vocalists who sang standards. Cole lost to Meshell Ndegeocello. The fellow nominees included Arooj Aftab with Vijay Iyer and Shahzad Ismaily, Kurt Elling with Charlie Hunter, and Cory Henry — a group that collectively represented the exact kind of music the Grammy infrastructure had never quite known how to file.
